Three lessons from fifteen years of running a freight dispatch desk

When I started dispatching in 2010, I believed the best dispatchers were the ones who never lost their cool. After fifteen years, I have changed my mind. The best dispatchers are the ones who tell the truth early.

Here are three lessons that have stayed with me.

First, bad news does not improve with age. A driver who is running two hours behind should say so immediately, not when the customer calls. Customers can forgive a delay. They rarely forgive surprises.

Second, write down every promise. Verbal commitments made on a busy Friday afternoon have a way of disappearing by Monday morning.

Third, learn the names of the people on the receiving dock. They control your day more than any software does.

What has your experience taught you about working with carriers and receivers? I would love to hear your thoughts in the comments.

Why Your Home Needs a Winter Roof Inspection

Many homeowners wait until a leak appears before calling a roofer, but by then the damage is often already inside the walls. A brief inspection before the first heavy snowfall can prevent costly repairs.

Start by checking for missing or curling shingles, which allow moisture to seep beneath the surface. Next, examine the flashing around chimneys and vents, since these are the most common leak points. Finally, make sure your gutters are clear. Clogged gutters can cause ice dams, which push water back under the roof edge.

A professional inspection usually takes less than an hour and costs between $150 and $300. Compared with an average repair bill of several thousand dollars, it is a worthwhile investment.

If you are unsure whether your roof is ready for winter, schedule an inspection this month, while the weather is still mild.

What Our Volunteers Taught Us This Year

When we opened the Eastside Community Pantry in January, we expected to serve about 200 families a month. By September, that number had reached 640. None of it would have been possible without our 85 volunteers.

Over the past year, they have taught us several important things. Consistency matters more than enthusiasm: a volunteer who shows up every second Tuesday is worth more than one who arrives once with great energy. Training matters, too. A twenty-minute orientation reduced our packing errors by half.

Most of all, we learned that people want to feel useful. When we gave volunteers real responsibility, such as managing the cold storage log, they stayed longer and brought their friends.

If you are thinking about volunteering, we would be glad to meet you. Our next orientation is on November 14.

Understanding the Basics of a Commercial Lease

If you are leasing retail space for the first time, the paperwork can feel overwhelming. Here are four terms worth understanding before you sign.

Base rent is the fixed amount you pay each month, usually quoted per square foot per year. Common area maintenance charges, often called CAM, cover shared costs such as parking lot upkeep and landscaping. A personal guarantee makes you individually responsible if the business cannot pay. Finally, the renewal option determines whether you can extend the lease and at what price.

Always have an attorney review the lease before signing, and ask the landlord for a breakdown of CAM charges from the previous year. These details can differ greatly between buildings and can significantly affect your costs.

A Short Guide to Preparing Your Manufacturing Floor for Audit Season

Audit season has a way of arriving sooner than expected. Teams that prepare steadily rather than at the last minute tend to have calmer, more productive audits.

Begin with documentation. Confirm that calibration records for every gauge are current and that operators can locate work instructions without searching. Next, walk the floor with fresh eyes. Look for unlabeled containers, blocked exits, and tools that lack designated storage. Finally, hold a brief practice interview with operators so they feel comfortable explaining their tasks.

A one-hour walkthrough each week for the month before the audit is usually enough to catch most issues. Small, consistent habits help far more than a frantic final weekend.

Cold Storage Receiving Procedure

Purpose: This procedure describes how to receive temperature-controlled shipments at the distribution center.

1. Verify the trailer seal number against the bill of lading before opening the doors.
2. Measure the product temperature using a calibrated probe thermometer. Take readings from at least three locations in the load.
3. Frozen products must be at or below -10 degrees Celsius. Chilled products must be between 0 and 5 degrees Celsius.
4. If any reading is outside these limits, do not unload. Notify the shift supervisor and complete a Non-Conformance Report.
5. Move accepted product into the appropriate cold room within 20 minutes of unloading.

Record all temperature readings in the receiving log and retain it for 24 months.

Patient Registration Guidelines

All new patients must complete registration before their first appointment. Front desk staff should follow the steps below.

Collect a government-issued photo identification and the patient's current insurance card. Scan both documents into the patient record. Confirm the patient's legal name, date of birth, and contact information, and ask whether the preferred language is English or another language so that interpreter services can be arranged.

Provide the Notice of Privacy Practices and obtain a signature. If the patient is under 18, a parent or legal guardian must sign on their behalf.

Verify insurance eligibility within two business days of the appointment. Any coverage issues should be reported to the billing office.

Expense Reimbursement Policy

Employees may be reimbursed for reasonable business expenses incurred while performing their duties. Expenses must be submitted within 30 days of the purchase date, accompanied by an itemized receipt.

Meals during business travel are reimbursed up to $65 per day. Lodging should be booked through the approved travel portal whenever possible. Mileage for personal vehicle use is reimbursed at the current federal rate.

Expenses over $500 require approval from a department head before purchase. Alcohol, personal entertainment, and fines are not reimbursable. Questions about this policy should be directed to the Accounts Payable team.

Lockout and Tagout Quick Reference

Before servicing any machine, follow these steps to ensure that energy sources are controlled.

First, notify all affected employees that the machine will be shut down. Second, shut down the machine using the normal stopping procedure. Third, isolate every energy source, including electrical, hydraulic, and pneumatic. Fourth, apply your personal lock and tag to each isolation point. Fifth, release or restrain any stored energy, then verify the machine is de-energized by attempting to start it.

Only the employee who applied a lock may remove it. If that person is unavailable, contact the safety manager for the approved removal process.

Most dock delays I've seen in the last decade were not caused by a lack of trucks or labor. They were caused by a lack of information. A driver shows up at 7 a.m., the appointment says 9, and nobody on the floor knows whether the trailer is loaded, staged, or still sitting in a yard two miles away.

We spent the first half of this year tracking every late arrival at our Dayton facility. The pattern was clear: roughly a third of delays came from paperwork that was never finished before the truck left the origin. Another third came from door assignments that changed after the driver had already checked in.

So we made two small changes. Dispatch now confirms the bill of lading before a truck leaves the yard, and door assignments are posted on a board the driver can see from the gate. Average detention dropped from 2.4 hours to 0.9 hours in eight weeks.

None of this required new software. It required someone to write down what was going wrong and then decide who owned each step.

Prior authorization is one of the least discussed sources of delay in outpatient care, and one of the most frustrating for patients. At our three clinics, we tracked how many scheduled imaging appointments were pushed back because authorization had not come through. The number was higher than any of us expected.

What we found was not complicated. Most denials came back for documentation the clinic already had but had not attached. The request forms were sent without the most recent progress note, or without the conservative therapy records that payers ask for by name.

We now run a short checklist before every submission, and our front desk staff have a direct line to the referring physician's office when something is missing. The result has been fewer denials and fewer calls from patients asking why their scan is still not booked.

If you run a practice and want to compare notes on your own process, I'm happy to talk.

I opened my shop with $11,000 and a used Singer. Three years later I still hand-check every seam on the returns pile, and I'm not going to pretend that's efficient.

What I got wrong early was thinking the fabric was the product. It isn't. The product is the fit, and fit depends on whether the person buying actually knows their measurements. Half my returns were people who ordered the medium because it was the one they always wore, not because it matched their chest.

So I wrote a sizing guide with real numbers and put it on the product page above the buy button. Returns dropped by about a third. Not dramatic, but it paid for the new cutting table.

Small shops don't need a clever growth plan. They need to figure out where the money leaks, and then stop it. For me the leak was a sentence I'd been too lazy to write.

Grid interconnection queues have become one of the quiet bottlenecks in the renewable energy buildout. A project that is financially sound on paper can wait several years for a study result, and the uncertainty around those timelines makes lenders cautious.

For developers working in the mid-Atlantic region, the most useful thing right now is to understand where their project sits relative to known upgrades. Substations with spare capacity move faster. Projects that bundle storage with generation often get clearer timelines because the utility can model them more precisely.

None of this makes the queue shorter. It does make planning more honest. Teams that build their schedule around the best available utility data, rather than the most optimistic one, tend to avoid the costly surprise of a missed interconnection date.

Every year our volunteer program receives more applications than we can place. For a long time we treated that as a good problem and moved on. This year we looked more closely at who was applying and why many of them dropped out before their first shift.

The answer was almost always logistics. Shifts were posted without clear start times. Parking near the food pantry was limited. And the orientation was scheduled on weekday mornings, which excluded people who worked hourly jobs.

We made three changes. We moved orientation to Saturday mornings, added a free shuttle from the transit stop, and started sending a text reminder the evening before every shift. In the first quarter, the share of applicants who completed a first shift rose from 38 percent to 61 percent.

Volunteer retention is not only about motivation. It is also about removing small barriers that make showing up hard.

When a small business applies for a loan, the lender is rarely asking whether the owner is capable. The lender is asking whether the cash flow will survive a slow quarter. Those are different questions, and most applications answer only the first one.

In our experience, the strongest applications include three things: a simple twelve-month cash flow forecast that the owner has actually tested against past seasons, a clear explanation of which costs can be cut without hurting revenue, and a realistic schedule for repayment that accounts for the worst month of the year rather than the average one.

None of this requires a finance degree. It requires an honest look at the numbers and a willingness to write down what would go wrong.

Owners who do this work before they apply tend to get better terms, and they also tend to sleep better afterward.
